desc:
The array nums is a mountain: strictly increasing up to a peak, then strictly decreasing (the peak is neither the first nor the last element). Values may repeat between the two slopes.

Each query is a pair [lo, hi] with lo ≤ hi. For every query, count how many elements x of nums satisfy lo ≤ x ≤ hi. Return the counts in query order.

With many queries, scanning the array per query is too slow in the worst case; answer each query in O(log n).
constraints: -10<sup>9</sup> ≤ nums[i], lo, hi ≤ 10<sup>9</sup>, and lo ≤ hi
nums is guaranteed to be a mountain array
hints: A count of values inside [lo, hi] equals (count of values ≤ hi) minus (count of values ≤ lo - 1). So one helper countAtMost(x) is enough.
The mountain splits into two sorted pieces at the peak: an ascending left part and a descending right part. Find the peak first with a binary search, then count in each piece separately.

In the ascending part, binary search the first index with value > x; everything before it counts. In the descending part, binary search the first index with value ≤ x; everything from it to the end counts.
editorial: Turn the range count into a difference of two prefix-style counts: countAtMost(hi) - countAtMost(lo - 1).

Compute countAtMost(x) on the mountain in O(log n). First locate the peak once (the usual binary search comparing nums[mid] with nums[mid + 1]). The part nums[0..peak] is ascending, so the elements ≤ x form a prefix; a binary search for the first value > x gives its length. The part nums[peak + 1..] is descending, so the elements ≤ x form a suffix; a binary search for the first value ≤ x gives its start, and the suffix length is n - start. Add both.
The peak search is done once, then each query costs O(log n). Total time is O(log n + q log n) and the extra space is O(1) besides the output.
